messages.subject: Simulating random data/landmarks around mean shapes + Identifying covariances introduced by GPA or combine.subsets
parts:
Hi all,
I’m hoping to get some help on two questions.
I’ve thought about them a lot and am feeling stuck.

First, the questions:
How (practically) could I simulate random data/landmarks around mean shapes?
More conceptually, could I use the data from Q1 to identify and account for covariance biases in a modularity analysis (using phylo.modularity) that might be introduced by performing GPAs on individual bones and then combining them with combine.subsets (without a second GPA during combine subsets).

Second, the background to these questions:
We recently had a paper reviewed where we performed GPAs on individual bones(vertebrae) for many species. After each vertebrae was aligned for all species, we then combined those vertebrae with combine.subsets. We did not perform a second GPA during implementation of combine.subset function (option GPA = FALSE), so that vertebrae were equally scaled in our analysis and to avoid introducing covariances that can mislead modularity analyses when modules are subsets of a common Procrustes superimposition (Cardini 2019).
Cardini, A. (2019). Integration and modularity in Procrustes shape data: is there a risk of spurious results?. Evolutionary Biology, 46(1), 90-105.

However, Cardini (2019) also pointed out that “the separate blocks approach may have appropriate rates of type I errors (no more false positives than expected by chance because of sampling error), but yet lead to large type II error rates (i.e., too many false negatives suggesting no integration when in fact it is there).”
Thus, Cardini speculates that although our chosen analysis avoids the pitfalls evidenced in their study, our analysis may have issues that they did not analytically explore.

A reviewer pointed out “the potential for covariances to be introduced by the superimposition (or even just the spacing of the landmarks). There may also be covariances introduced or removed by the combine.subsets function.”

And they suggested “that you simulate random data around the mean shapes, and run the analyses of modularity on those data, to determine whether those too yield an apparently modular signal like the one you discerned in your data. I found that all the models that I fit were favored over the null, and some models were also favored over others when fit to the simulated data.  If you also find that covariances are introduced by superimposition, and either introduced or removed by combining subsets, you might reconsider what the appropriate null hypothesis should be when testing for modularity.”

However, I’m having trouble figuring out 1) how to simulate the data and 2) whether and how I could use those simulated data to find a more “appropriate null hypothesis”. Cardini (2019) identified biases using many datasets and I would just be simulating data around my single example dataset. Is this even sufficient? Or should I just be providing clear caveats and explanations of this potential biases in our discussion?

I realize this is a larger question that might go beyond the scope of this group. But I’m curious if anyone has performed similar simulations or has ideas on how to test for these biases and interpret the results.

For those that made it this far in the message, THANK YOU for your consideration.
I really appreciate any ideas/help.

I’m happy to clarify anything via group messages or by any other chat method.

parts:
Molly,

 

Your post hits upon an area for which considerable theoretical work is still required: Cardini 2019 is hardly the last word on the subject. In fact, just last week I was diving into conceptual issues related to the broader topic for which said paper only superficially glances at. Hopefully my deep-dive will turn up something of a more general solution to the broader set of problems here (there are several, not just ‘separate’ GPA vs. single), but that will take a while for me to sort out. In the meantime, to help you move forward with your particular empirical study, here are a few thoughts that may be helpful.

 

First, I totally agree that when one has several empirical moving parts, it is a good idea to simulate some data, so that you can control for one aspect of the study (true landmark variation/covariation) while examining the effects of another (e.g., landmark spacing or other components).  The procedure you outlines is on the right track: simulate data around the mean shape to generate a ‘sample’ of representative observations, which are then used in some down-stream pipeline.  A script to do this is below. 

 

NOTE: a very important step – and one that some folks often miss or otherwise do not appreciate – is the scaling of the random input variation relative to the size of your object matters a great deal.  One has to get this just right, or any analysis, type I error, type II error test, etc. is simply GIGO (garbage-in-garbage-out).  As your simulations are based on your empirical study, I recommend scaling the random variation you generate by the observed variation in your sample.

 

In the script below, I do it both ways: first the naïve simulation where the scaling step is ignored, and then with scaling relative to actual total variation. The plots make the difference blindingly obvious. 

 

###

library(geomorph)

library(MASS)

 

data(plethodon)

manders <- gpagen(plethodon$land)

mn <- mshape(manders$coords)

n <-dim(plethodon$land)[3]

p <- manders$p; k <- manders$k

 

var.obs <- mean(diag(var(two.d.array(manders$coords))))  #average landmark-coordinate variation in observed data

 

sim.1 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(1,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #naive simulation

sim.2 <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=matrix(t(mn)),Sigma=diag(var.obs,p*k)),p=p,k=k)   #variance-informed simulation

 

plotAllSpecimens(sim.1)                   

plotAllSpecimens(sim.2)    

###

 

Good luck with your study!!!

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams (he/him)

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/dcadams/

parts:
Dear Molly,

I was in the process of providing an example when Dean beat me to it, but I’ll provide mine, anyway, because it has a step to not only create random data but create many sets of random data, from which one might create a distribution of modularity effect sizes created from isotropic data.  The goal here is to create many modularity outcomes, assuming the covariances within modules are due to nothing more than GPA.  CAVEATS: I have not given a lot of thought to the appropriateness of this as a method but merely suggest it as an aid for simulating random data.  Also, by using verbose = TRUE in gpagen, it is possible to skip a couple of steps that Dean suggested, as it creates a covariance matrix for different points.  (Also Dean used the mean of variances to apply to all points.  I use each point's variances.  Neither is correct nor incorrect, without additional research.  Getting these variances post-GPA and then simulating data on which GPA will again be performed makes this process a little challenging.)

Script below - Mike

# Using plethspecies example:

library(geomorph)
data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land, verbose = TRUE)    # verbose = TRUE, provides VCV
land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B") 

MT <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpa$coords, partition.gp=land.gps, 
                       phy=plethspecies$phy, 
                       CI = FALSE, iter=999)
summary(MT) # Test summary

Mean <- Y.gpa$consensus # mean config
Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
Var <- diag(diag(Y.gpa$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
n <- length(Y.gpa$Csize)
p <- Y.gpa$p
k <- Y.gpa$k

# One permutation of random data:
library(MASS)

IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)

# These should look nearly indistinguishable:

plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpa$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))
dimnames(IsoCoords) <- dimnames(Y.gpa$coords)
Y.gpar <- gpagen(IsoCoords)
plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpar$coords, plot.param = list(mean.cex = 0.5))

# Modularity test done on isotropic random data

MTr <- phylo.modularity(Y.gpar$coords, partition.gp=land.gps, 
                       phy=plethspecies$phy, 
                       CI = FALSE, iter=999)
summary(MTr)

# A function for multiple permutations of isotropic data
# This will make a list of random permutations
# This expects that GPA was performed with verbose = TRUE

makeIsoCoords <- function(GPA, permutations){
  coords <- GPA$coords
  n <- length(GPA$Csize)
  p <- GPA$p
  k <- GPA$k
  Mean <- GPA$consensus # mean config
  Mean.vect <- as.vector(t(Mean)) # make the mean into a vector
  Var <- diag(diag(GPA$points.VCV)) # Isotropic variances from GPA VCV
  result <- lapply(1:permutations, function(.){
    IsoCoords <- mvrnorm(n, mu = Mean.vect, Sigma = Var)
    IsoCoords <- arrayspecs(IsoCoords, p, k)
    GPAr <- gpagen(IsoCoords, print.progress = FALSE)
    rCoords <- GPAr$coords
    dimnames(rCoords) <- dimnames(GPA$coords)
    rCoords
  })
  
  return(result)
}

# Example for how to get 100 effect sizes from random data:

randomCoords <- makeIsoCoords(Y.gpa, 100)

getZ <- function(coords){
  MT <- phylo.modularity(coords, partition.gp=land.gps, 
                         phy=plethspecies$phy, 
                         CI = FALSE, iter=999, print.progress = FALSE)
  return(MT$Z)
}

Zs <- sapply(randomCoords, getZ) # get 100 Z scores

summary(Zs) # make a five-point summary of the Zs

# One could compare their observed result to the distribution of Zs made from isotropic data
# If modularity is more pronounced in the observed case than what is commonly generated
# from random data, it would suggest the effect is not merely due to GPA, per Cardini

Hi Dean and Mike, 
Thank you so very much for your help here!
I am really thankful for this code and even more thankful for the time you both put into thinking about this. 

I'm glad you have similar thoughts about what should be done - yes, I should simulate data to assess introduced bias with all the moving parts BUT Cardini has some caveats and there is a lot more (that goes beyond the scope of our paper) that needs to be done to fully address the concerns reviewers (and Cardini) raise. 

I will try these simulations and add some notes to our discussion about outstanding issues that go beyond the scope of this paper.
I'll let you know if things seem GIGO 🙂 Or if the results turn up interesting. 

This paper has been our most ambitious geometric morphometrics project to-date, but all the moving parts have created a fun learning experience that is continuing through the review process. 
Thank you to the geomorph community! The project wouldn't have been nearly as fun (or possible) without this package!

Hi all,
I’m hoping to get some help on two questions.
I’ve thought about them a lot and am feeling stuck. 

First, the questions:
How (practically) could I simulate random data/landmarks around mean shapes?
More conceptually, could I use the data from Q1 to identify and account for covariance biases in a modularity analysis (using phylo.modularity) that might be introduced by performing GPAs on individual bones and then combining them with combine.subsets (without a second GPA during combine subsets).

Second, the background to these questions:
We recently had a paper reviewed where we performed GPAs on individual bones(vertebrae) for many species. After each vertebrae was aligned for all species, we then combined those vertebrae with combine.subsets. We did not perform a second GPA during implementation of combine.subset function (option GPA = FALSE), so that vertebrae were equally scaled in our analysis and to avoid introducing covariances that can mislead modularity analyses when modules are subsets of a common Procrustes superimposition (Cardini 2019).
Cardini, A. (2019). Integration and modularity in Procrustes shape data: is there a risk of spurious results?. Evolutionary Biology, 46(1), 90-105.

However, Cardini (2019) also pointed out that “the separate blocks approach may have appropriate rates of type I errors (no more false positives than expected by chance because of sampling error), but yet lead to large type II error rates (i.e., too many false negatives suggesting no integration when in fact it is there).”
Thus, Cardini speculates that although our chosen analysis avoids the pitfalls evidenced in their study, our analysis may have issues that they did not analytically explore.

A reviewer pointed out “the potential for covariances to be introduced by the superimposition (or even just the spacing of the landmarks). There may also be covariances introduced or removed by the combine.subsets function.”

And they suggested “that you simulate random data around the mean shapes, and run the analyses of modularity on those data, to determine whether those too yield an apparently modular signal like the one you discerned in your data. I found that all the models that I fit were favored over the null, and some models were also favored over others when fit to the simulated data.  If you also find that covariances are introduced by superimposition, and either introduced or removed by combining subsets, you might reconsider what the appropriate null hypothesis should be when testing for modularity.”

However, I’m having trouble figuring out 1) how to simulate the data and 2) whether and how I could use those simulated data to find a more “appropriate null hypothesis”. Cardini (2019) identified biases using many datasets and I would just be simulating data around my single example dataset. Is this even sufficient? Or should I just be providing clear caveats and explanations of this potential biases in our discussion?

I realize this is a larger question that might go beyond the scope of this group. But I’m curious if anyone has performed similar simulations or has ideas on how to test for these biases and interpret the results.
